---
title: 'Add pipelines from the repository'
status: implemented
description: 'Let config files in the repository become pipelines, and see when a pipeline file is missing, invalid, or lost its workflow.'
---

Oore looks for config files in the project's repository on its default branch.
Each file can become a pipeline with one click, or on its own when the project
adds pipelines automatically. Each pipeline then shows whether its file is
usable.

## Where Oore looks

On the project's default branch, Oore reads these files:

- `.oore.yaml` and `.oore.yml`
- any other root file named `.oore.<name>.yaml` or `.oore.<name>.yml`, such as
  `.oore.release.yaml`
- YAML files in `.oore/` and one folder below it, such as `.oore/ci.yaml` or
  `.oore/ios/beta.yaml`

Oore reads at most 16 files of up to 128 KB each. When a repository has more,
the list says so.

Oore keeps what it found for the commit it read. A push to the default branch
that changes one of these paths reads the branch again, in the background, so
it never delays or fails the webhook delivery. Oore also reads the branch when
a project is created and when its source or default branch changes.

## Add a pipeline for a file

1. Open the project's **Pipelines** tab.
2. Under **Found in repository**, find the file. The list shows only files no
   pipeline uses yet, with the workflows each one defines.
3. Select **Add**. Select **Add all** to add every valid file at once.

The new pipeline builds from that file and is named after it:
`.oore.release.yaml` becomes **Release**, and `.oore/ios/beta.yaml` becomes
**Ios beta**. Rename it on the pipeline's **Edit** page.

A file that does not parse shows **Invalid** with its first error, and cannot
be added until it is fixed.

Select **Refresh** to read the branch now, for example after a push that Oore
did not receive.

You can also select **Add pipeline**. Under **Start from**, Oore lists the
files it found, those no pipeline uses first, and marks the others **In use**.

## Add pipelines automatically

Turn on **Add pipelines from the repository automatically** in the project's
**Settings** tab. Each time Oore reads the default branch, a valid file that
was not there the last time, and that no pipeline uses, becomes a pipeline.

- New projects have it on. Projects created before this setting have it off.
- A file Oore had already seen is not added again, so a pipeline you delete
  stays deleted. Add it from **Found in repository** if you want it back.
- A pipeline added this way has default settings. The file's `on` decides
  which pushes, pull requests, and tags start it; without `on` it starts only
  when you run it, on a schedule, or from the API.

## Pipeline health

Each pipeline row shows its file and its health on the default branch. The
pipeline page shows a banner when the file needs attention.

| Health               | Meaning                                                                                  |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **File OK**          | The file exists and parses, and defines the pipeline's workflow if it picks one          |
| **No file**          | The file is not on the default branch, so builds use the settings saved in Oore          |
| **Invalid file**     | The file exists but does not parse; builds of this pipeline fail                         |
| **Workflow missing** | The file no longer defines the workflow the pipeline picks; builds of that workflow fail |

Health comes from the last read of the default branch, never from a call to
GitHub or GitLab while the page loads. A pipeline shows no health until Oore
has read the repository once.
The API returns it as the pipeline's `health`; see
[Health](/reference/config/pipeline-settings#health).

## The config path

A pipeline's config path always names the file it builds from. A pipeline
with `.oore.yaml` still reads `.oore.yml` when only that file exists. The
first read of the default branch writes `.oore.yml` on pipelines that relied
on that, so the path shows the file in use.

The API field `config_path_explicit` is deprecated. Oore ignores it on create
and update and always returns `true`.
